lead: REST is a way to design a web API around things, not actions. A book, a user and an order are resources. Each resource gets a URL made of plural nouns, and the HTTP method says what to do with it. POST /books creates a book, GET /books/7 reads book 7, and JSON carries the data in both directions. Browsers, mobile apps and React pages all call such APIs. The style exists because one small set of methods and status codes lets any client talk to any server without a private vocabulary.
prereq: You need: Express routing and handlers from 6.4, and the HTTP methods and status codes from Unit 1.

blocks.text: A resource is a named thing: a book, a customer, an order. A collection is a resource that holds many items. /books is the collection; /books/7 is one item inside it. Use plural nouns and no verbs. /getBooks is wrong because GET already says read; /books?author=gupta is right for filtering.
Five methods cover CRUD. CRUD means Create, Read, Update, Delete.

The id belongs in the path. The body holds the data, not the identity. POST /books returns the new item and a Location header. A header is a name-value line in a request or response. PUT replaces the whole item; a field you leave out is cleared or set to its default. PATCH changes only the fields you send. A common exam mistake is using PUT for a partial update.

A method is safe if the client is not asking the server to change any resource. GET is safe, even though the server may still write a log line. A method is idempotent if sending the same request twice leaves the same final state as sending it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. PUT and DELETE are not safe because they change state. POST is neither: two POST /books calls create two books, with ids 7 and 8. PUT /books/7 twice still leaves one book 7. DELETE /books/7 twice leaves it deleted; the second call may return 404, but the state is the same. PATCH is not safe, and it is not guaranteed idempotent, because the patch document may describe a change relative to the current value (for example 'increment stock by 1').
Status codes are three-digit numbers that summarise the result.

Meaning
When to use

not logged in or bad token
clashes with existing state, e.g. duplicate email

blocks.text: Use 201 on create, not 200. Use 204 on delete when there is nothing to return.

JSON is a text format for objects and arrays. Content-Type: application/json tells the server that the request body is JSON. Accept: application/json asks the server for a JSON response. Express needs the express.json() middleware to read JSON bodies, then res.json() sends JSON back. See 6.4.

GET /books returns an array; GET /books/7 returns one object. Query strings, the part after ?, filter and page: /books?author=gupta&page=2&limit=10. State limit and page in the API documentation. Version the path: /api/v1/books. A new incompatible shape goes to /api/v2.

REST is stateless: each request carries everything needed, such as the token. The server does not remember the previous request. This lets any server in a pool answer any request. Database work is in 6.6; protecting routes is in 6.8.

examples.question: Design the CRUD routes for a books API and give the success status for each. Then say how many books exist after POST /books is sent twice with the same JSON, and name the safe and idempotent methods.
steps: Create: POST /books with JSON. The database returns id 7. Respond 201 Created, Location: /books/7, and the new book.
List: GET /books returns 200 OK with an array of books.
Read one: GET /books/7 returns 200 OK with one object. GET /books/99 for a missing book returns 404 Not Found.
Replace: PUT /books/7 with the full JSON object returns 200 OK and the replaced book.
Delete: DELETE /books/7 returns 204 No Content with an empty body.
Safe methods: GET only. Idempotent methods: GET, PUT and DELETE. POST is neither safe nor idempotent, and PATCH is not safe either. Two identical POSTs create id 7 and id 8, so 2 books exist.
examples.answer: Create returns 201, list and read return 200, a missing read returns 404, replace returns 200, delete returns 204, and two identical POSTs leave 2 books. Only GET is safe; GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is neither.
examples.check:
routes = [
    ("POST", "/books", 201),
    ("GET", "/books", 200),
    ("GET", "/books/7", 200),
    ("GET", "/books/99", 404),
    ("PUT", "/books/7", 200),
    ("DELETE", "/books/7", 204),
]
for method, path, code in routes:
    print(code)
posts = 2
books = posts * 1
print(books)

traps: Using PUT for a partial update; that is PATCH. PUT replaces the whole resource.
Writing verbs into the URL such as /getBooks; use the method plus a plural noun, such as GET /books.
Returning 200 instead of 201 on create. Create should return 201 with a Location header.
Putting the id in the JSON body instead of the path. The URL /books/7 identifies the resource.
Saying POST is idempotent or DELETE is not. Two POSTs create two books; two DELETEs leave the same final state.

quiz.q: Which HTTP method creates a resource, and which status code should it return?
quiz.a: POST creates a resource and should return 201 Created, with a Location header.

quiz.q: Why is POST not idempotent while PUT is?
quiz.a: Two POST /books calls create two new books with different ids. Two PUT /books/7 calls replace the same book 7, so the final state is the same.

quiz.q: A client sends DELETE /books/7 twice. The first returns 204. What does the second probably return, and what is the final state?
quiz.a: The second probably returns 404 Not Found because book 7 is already gone. The final state is still that book 7 does not exist.

quiz.q: A route PUT /books/7 accepts only {title}. What is wrong, and what should change?
quiz.a: PUT should replace the whole book, so a title-only body is a partial update. Change the route to PATCH /books/7 for partial updates, or send the full object with PUT.

quiz.q: Which status code means not logged in, and which means logged in but not allowed?
quiz.a: 401 Unauthorized means not logged in or a bad token. 403 Forbidden means logged in but not allowed.

quiz.q: Write the URL to list page 2 with 10 books per page, filtered by author gupta, API version 1.
Why should the id not be in the JSON body for PUT /books/7?
quiz.a: The URL already identifies book 7. An id in the body can disagree with the path, so the server would have two identities for one resource. The path is the authority.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, OpenAPI describes REST endpoints so client code and docs can be generated. Idempotency keys let a client retry a POST safely; a UPI payment retry can otherwise create two debits. GraphQL and gRPC solve overlapping problems with different trade-offs. Search for OpenAPI specification, idempotency keys, JSON:API and HTTP caching next.
